content.title: How much does Artemis II cost—and who pays for it?
content.text: The Science Of Space MunchingAt the heart of every astronaut's meal plan, the humble tortilla. Tortillas have long been a practical staple in spaceflight because they are versatile, easy to eat in microgravity, and create far fewer crumbs than bread. Crumbs in space aren't just annoying, they're dangerous. Floating particles can drift into gadgetry and interfere with electrical systems, or even end up in the eyes or noses of the astronauts, causing health issues. Mission specialist Jeremy Hansen was caught hilariously chasing rogue crumbs through the air, proof that even in space, snacking comes with consequences. The Artemis II crew packed a staggering 58 tortillas for the 10-day trip. A Menu Fit For Space ExplorersPrepare yourself: the four crew members, Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Jeremy Hansen and Christina Koch, have a selection of 189 different menu items to choose from on their journey around the moon. Not a spaceship cafeteria nightmare, not emergency rations but actual variety.The menu reads like a surprisingly upscale restaurant. Astronauts can enjoy macaroni and cheese, beef brisket, and broccoli au gratin. There's breakfast sausage with granola and blueberries, along with vegetable quiche. Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen enjoys five Canadian food products to remind him of home, including wild keta salmon bites, shrimp curry, strawberry lavender superseed cereal, maple cream cookies, and, of course, maple syrup. For those with a sweet tooth, there are several desserts, mostly cookies and chocolate. And yes, there's hot sauce. In total, there are five varieties of hot sauce onboard, because even in space, spice matters. And in Christina Koch's own words to a group of Canadian school children about mac and cheese packed in bags, "we do have to eat our vegetables even in space," Koch told the children, "but don't worry, they do give us mac and cheese."Much of the food arrives dehydrated and freeze-dried, a flat, crinkled pouch that looks nothing like dinner. Add 75ml of hot water from Orion's onboard dispenser, wait ten to fifteen minutes, and somehow, green beans emerge. The crew reanimates their meals using water and heat, careful not to tear the tops of the packaging all the way off, an astronaut custom, to prevent pieces of trash from floating away. There's More Food In SpaceFor warmth, they rely on a game-changing new gadget: a briefcase-style food warmer, a luxury the Apollo missions never had. Astronauts can warm up to 12 packages of food at the same time, in under an hour. Coffee lovers, rejoice, sort of. NASA has allotted 43 cups of coffee for the crew, roughly 10 cups per astronaut across the 10-day mission. Beyond coffee, astronauts have access to more than 10 types of beverages, including green tea, lemonade, cocoa, apple cider, and a mango-peach smoothie. Perhaps the most human detail of all? Eating together is something the crew actively values. "Eating together really resonates with me. I think it's just a human thing," said Hansen. Even 240,000 miles from Earth, dinner is still dinner, and apparently, it's better than some people's Tuesday night takeout.Stay updated with the latest and breaking news on Times Now.
